title: After the Flood: Two Towns Clean Up

sentences.text: Two mountain towns on the Georgia-Tennessee border are still cleaning up after flash flooding earlier this month.
sentences.soundNote: "Cleaning up" is said as one smooth phrase. The stress is on CLEAN.

sentences.text: Torrential rain fell overnight on November 4, as much as 11 inches in a matter of hours.
sentences.soundNote: "November 4" is read as "November fourth," and "11" as "eleven." "Matter of" is quick and light.

sentences.text: The Ocoee River rose more than 15 feet, a record high.
sentences.soundNote: "Ocoee" sounds like "oh-KOH-ee." "15" is "fifteen" - listen for the long "teen."

sentences.text: In the middle of the night, residents of McCaysville were ordered to leave their homes.
sentences.soundNote: In this clip, "middle of the night" is read clearly, word by word. In fast conversation it can sound like "mid-luh-thuh-night."

sentences.text: Across the two states, crews carried out more than 160 rescues.
sentences.soundNote: "160" is read as "one hundred sixty." "Carried out" is read clearly here.

sentences.text: The river crested, or peaked, around 6 a.m. at just over 18 feet, breaking a record set in 1990.
sentences.soundNote: "6 a.m." sounds like "six-ay-em." "1990" is "nineteen ninety." There is a small pause around "or peaked."

sentences.text: Forecasters say storms stalled briefly over the mountains, and steep terrain funneled the water into creeks and the river.
sentences.soundNote: Listen for the past endings: "stalled" and "funneled" both end in a soft "d" sound.

sentences.text: Georgia's governor declared a state of emergency in four counties, and the bridges linking the two towns were closed.
sentences.soundNote: "State of" sounds like "stay-duv" in this clip. The T goes soft and "of" hooks on.

sentences.text: When the water receded, dozens of homes and downtown shops were left coated in mud.
sentences.soundNote: "Coated in mud" runs together. It sounds like "KOH-dih-din mud."

sentences.text: In the wake of the flood, volunteers have been helping with the cleanup in both towns.
sentences.soundNote: The K in "wake" slides into "of." It sounds like "WAY-kuv."

sentences.text: As of late last week, one town remained under a boil-water advisory, and federal teams had begun surveying the damage.
sentences.soundNote: "Boil-water advisory" has the main stress on BOIL and on VI: ad-VI-so-ry.

sentences.text: The river is back within its banks, but for both towns, the cleanup is far from over.
sentences.soundNote: In this clip, "far from over" is read clearly. The strongest word is "far."

vocab.meaning: sudden flooding that happens very quickly after heavy rain
vocab.example: Flash flooding closed three roads in less than an hour.

vocab.meaning: falling very fast and in huge amounts (about rain)
vocab.example: We drove home slowly through torrential rain.

vocab.meaning: in only a few hours; surprisingly fast
vocab.example: The tickets sold out in a matter of hours.

vocab.meaning: to do a planned job or task
vocab.example: Doctors carried out the operation on Monday.

vocab.meaning: (of a river) to reach its highest level before going down
vocab.example: The river is expected to crest on Friday night.

vocab.meaning: (of a storm) to stop moving and stay over one place
vocab.example: The storm stalled over the coast for two days.

vocab.meaning: to push something through a narrow space
vocab.example: The fence funnels fans toward the main gate.

vocab.meaning: to officially announce a serious situation that needs special action
vocab.example: The mayor declared a state of emergency after the storm.

vocab.meaning: (of water) to slowly move back or go down
vocab.example: We could not go home until the water receded.

vocab.meaning: after something serious, and because of it
vocab.example: Prices rose in the wake of the drought.

vocab.meaning: an official warning to boil tap water before drinking it
vocab.example: A broken pipe led to a boil-water advisory for the whole city.

vocab.meaning: not close to finished; with a lot still to do
vocab.example: The game is far from over - there are twenty minutes left.

moreFromEmily.note: In fast conversation these words often run together. In this news clip, the reporter reads each word clearly.
In casual speech the D can slide into "out." In this news clip, the two words are read clearly.
In casual speech "from" gets short and joins "over." In this news clip, the phrase is read clearly.

moreFromEmily.example: Staff funneled the crowd through one door.

moreFromEmily.meaning: to reach the highest level before going down
moreFromEmily.example: Officials expect the river to crest tomorrow morning.

moreFromEmily.meaning: to stop moving and stay in one place
moreFromEmily.example: The rain band stalled over the valley all night.
